info.bio:
Pete Townshend es uno de los músicos que más influencia han dado a la historia del Rock. Ha sido el guitarrista y líder de The Who desde sus inicios, siendo el compositor y arreglista de sus mejores canciones. 

Su obra maestra es sin duda la ópera rock Tommy, la cuál fue llevada al cine y en la cuál actuaron entre otros Eric Clapton, Jack Nicholson, Tina Turner, Elton John, Ann Margaret y The Who, siendo Roger Daltrey quien interpretó a Tommy.

scenes.name: Mods
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Hacia 1964-1965 los mods eran el culto juvenil británico más identificable: no la mayoría de adolescentes, sino el subgrupo que marcaba estilos y gastaba el dinero en ropa, discos, scooters y pastillas, con un relevo de modas maníaco («esto pasó de moda hace tres semanas»). Peter Laurie los vio como estaciones emisoras de un solo hombre, la primera generación que vivía conscientemente en un mundo de comunicaciones de masas; Townshend, como un sistema enteramente masculino. Heredaron de los beatniks las pastillas y las sesiones de toda la noche, cambiando el trad por la música negra americana de baile. Las batallas con los rockers de la primavera de 1964 trajeron titulares sobre «pequeños Césares de serrín».
scenes.family: Juventud, moda y medios: Swinging London, radio pirata

scenes.name: Arte autodestructivo y happenings
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: La violencia como martillo y no como espejo. Gustav Metzger, cuyas clases en la Ealing Art School inspiraron a Pete Townshend a destrozar guitarras, quería monumentos al poder humano de destruir toda vida, «a Hiroshima». En septiembre de 1966 organizó en Londres el Destruction in Art Symposium con cien artistas de dieciocho países (Ralph Ortiz destrozando un sillón de club, Hermann Nitsch eviscerando corderos, John Latham, Yoko Ono) en un solar bombardeado de Portobello Road; Metzger acabó acusado de exhibición indecente. Allan Kaprow enseñaba en disco a hacer un happening que no se supiera si era arte o vida, y Life dedicaba su portada al «arte LSD». Situaciones, provocaciones, autodestrucción, disturbios: la portada carnicera de los Beatles, la televisión quemada de los Provos y las guitarras rotas de los Who eran provocaciones del mismo orden, una exigencia de que el espectador reaccionara.
scenes.family: Vanguardia: Warhol, Velvet, free jazz, arte

scenes.name: Protometal: volumen, distorsión y moteros
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Los precursores que aportan piezas sueltas del código: el volumen como estética (Blue Cheer, MC5), el sonido de guitarra grueso y distorsionado (los Kinks en «You Really Got Me»), la contundencia de los Who en directo (Townshend presume de que Live at Leeds engendró «ese objeto grosero y asqueroso que fue Led Zeppelin») y la iconografía motera de «Born to Be Wild» de Steppenwolf, cuyo verso «heavy metal thunder» dio nombre al género. Algunos críticos estadounidenses defienden a Iron Butterfly, Steppenwolf o Blue Cheer como primera banda de heavy. En 1971 la crítica ya usa el término: Mike Saunders, en Creem, dice que Sir Lord Baltimore domina «todos los trucos del heavy metal».
scenes.family: Raíces: blues rock, psicodelia y hard rock

scenes.name: Cantautores de los setenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: James Taylor se convierte, misteriosamente, en el prototipo del cantautor de los setenta; Carole King, Carly Simon y Don McLean, sobrevalorados. Las innovaciones llegan del oeste: Randy Newman y sus viñetas urbanas con fusión de estilos populares, Shawn Phillips, J.J. Cale y su estilo «laid-back», Gram Parsons, Emmylou Harris, Roger McGuinn, Jackson Browne (Late For The Sky) y, sobre todo, Tom Waits, discípulo de Beefheart y cronista de marginados (Swordfishtrombones, Rain Dogs). Excéntricos como Todd Rundgren y Annette Peacock; en Gran Bretaña, Peter Hammill, Anthony Moore, Richard Thompson, Robert Calvert, John Cale, Kevin Coyne, Elton John y los ex Beatles. El realismo de Bruce Springsteen, verdadero heredero de Woody Guthrie y del blues, y la escuela italiana de cantautores (De André, Guccini, Battisti, Sorrenti).

podcast.title: Commissioning Marshall Amps (1962)
podcast.body: In 1962, Pete Townshend, a regular customer of Jim Marshall, requested a custom-built amplifier that would be "bigger and louder than the American Fender amps that he had been using." Townshend's explicit instruction was, "I don't want to hear the crowd," leading Marshall to develop more powerful amplification technology that was crucial for the evolving sound of rock. "Pete Townsend of The Who, asked Marshall to build an amp that was bigger and louder than the American Fender amps that he had been using."

podcast.title: "I Want My MTV" Campaign
podcast.body: Pete Townshend was one of the prominent artists who appeared in promos for the "I Want My MTV" campaign. This highly effective campaign encouraged people to call their local cable companies to demand that they carry the new channel, significantly expanding MTV's reach and power across the US. "Promos like this began to run constantly on MTV featuring the police, Pat Benatar, Pete Townsend, Cindy Loper, Billy Eidle, and even David Bowie."

podcast.title: Accidental Instrument Destruction as a Trademark
podcast.body: In 1964, while playing at the Railway Tavern in London, Pete Townsend accidentally broke the headstock of his new Rickenbacker guitar on a low ceiling. His subsequent frustration led him to intentionally smash the guitar and his amplifier, an act that was popular with the audience and became a regular part of The Who's performances, eventually defining their stage persona for a time. "Pete Townsend raised his brand new Rikin' Backer guitar too high and smashed the headstock into the ceiling. He was annoyed and decided to make a spectacle of his frustration and hammered the guitar into the stage in his amp until it was nothing but splinters."

podcast.body: Pete Townshend is listed among the famous musicians who visited Manie's Music in New York City to purchase gear. The store was a crucial stop for touring musicians. "Customers included the Beatles and Pete Townsend and Bob Dylan and literally thousands more."

podcast.title: Feedback Integration
podcast.body: Around the same time The Beatles were discovering how to use feedback, Pete Townshend of The Who was also independently exploring and discovering ways to incorporate feedback into his guitar playing, making it a deliberate part of his sound. "Meanwhile, Pete Townsend of the Who was discovering ways of incorporating feedback into his playing."

podcast.title: First Generation Guitar Hero
podcast.body: Pete Townshend is listed among the first to be declared a "guitar hero," recognized for his seemingly supernatural mastery of the electric guitar. "Pete Townsend... They were among the first to be declared guitar heroes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Rock Opera Credit
podcast.body: Pete Townshend is credited with creating the first rock opera, "A Quick One While He's Away," a 10-minute song with six movements recorded for The Who's 1966 album *A Quick One*. This ambitious composition established a precedent for the rock opera format. "And it is Townsend who was credited with the first rock opera a quick one while he's away."

podcast.title: Initial Impression of Pinball Wizard
podcast.body: Despite its success and influence, Pete Townshend initially considered "Pinball Wizard" to be "a clumsy attempt at songwriting." He was unsure about the track's quality even though it was written to gain the favor of critic Nick Cohn. "Townsend himself was not sure. And actually initially considered pinball wizard to be kind of a clumsy attempt at songwriting."

xref.title: Backstage Rider – Pre-Show Nap Provision for Pete Townshend
xref.body: The Who's tour rider included a provision for Pete Townshend, who liked to take a nap before shows. To facilitate this, a large queen or king-sized bed with fine linens was required to be supplied in his dressing room. "To facilitate that, a large queen or king bed with fine linens was to be supplied in a dressing room."

xref.title: Campaigns for Major Artists
xref.body: During her tenure as an executive, Margo Netts was instrumental in working on marketing and promotional campaigns for a wide array of prominent artists, including Stevie Nicks, Pete Townshend, ABBA, and Hall & Oates. Her influence helped shape the careers of many popular acts. "She worked on campaigns for everyone from Stevie Nicks to Pete Townsend to Abba to Holland Oats."

xref.title: Challenge to Design Louder Amplifiers
xref.body: Jim Marshall was consistently approached by musicians like Pete Townshend and Ritchie Blackmore, who expressed a strong desire for bigger, more powerful, and louder amplifiers. They challenged him to design an amp with specific sound and flexibility requirements. "And the one thing that they always talked about, the one thing they always pushed Jim for was a bigger, more powerful, and louder amplifier."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Guitar Legends
xref.body: His innovative guitar playing style, particularly his use of power chords, directly influenced iconic guitarists such as Jimmy Page and Pete Townshend, who picked up the guitar in part because of his sound. "Jimmy Page, Pete Townsend, guys like that picked up the guitar in part because of Link Ray."
